prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’m back again scrutinizing the Milky Way of your ultrasound, scanning the dark matter, the nothingness, that now the heads say is chockablock with quarks and squarks, gravitons and gravatini, photons and photinos. Our sprout, who art there inside the spacecraft of your Ma, the time capsule of this printout, hurling and whirling towards us, it’s all daft on this earth. Our alien who art in the heavens, our Martian, our little green man, we’re anxious to make contact, to ask divers questions about the heavendom you hail from, to discuss the whole shebang of the beginning and end, the pre-big bang untime before you forget the why and lie of thy first place. And, our friend, to say Welcome, that we mean no harm, we’d die for you even, that we pray you’re not here to subdue us, that we’d put away our ray guns, missiles, attitude and share our world with you, little big head, if only you stay.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Milky, Way, Our

outputs.L1:
I find myself once again scrutinizing the Milky Way of your ultrasound, scanning the dark matter, the nothingness that, the heads now say, is chockablock with quarks and squarks, gravitons and gravatini, photons and photinos.  

Our sprout, who art there inside the spacecraft of your Ma, within the time capsule of this printout, hurling and whirling toward us: it is all daft on this earth.  

Our alien who art in the heavens, our Martian, our little green man, we are anxious to make contact—to ask divers questions about the heavendom from which you hail, to discuss the whole shebang of the beginning and the end, the pre–Big Bang untime before you forget the why and lie of thy first place.  

And, our friend, to say: Welcome. We mean no harm. We would die for you, even. We pray you are not here to subdue us; we would put away our ray guns, missiles, and attitude, and share our world with you, little big head—if only you stay.
outputs.L2: Once more I find myself examining the galaxy inside your ultrasound, peering through its darkness and apparent void—the emptiness that the experts now insist is crowded with quarks and squarks, gravitons and gravatini, photons and photinos. Our small shoot, lodged within the vessel of your mother, preserved in the time-capsule image of this printout, spinning and rushing toward us: everything here on Earth is absurd. Our stranger from the skies, our Martian, our tiny green visitor, we are eager to establish contact, to ask all kinds of questions about the celestial place you come from, to talk over the entire business of origins and endings, the timeless pre–Big Bang before you lose memory of the reason and the fiction of your first home. And, dear companion, we want to tell you: Welcome. We intend you no injury; we would even give our lives for you. We hope you have not come to conquer us. We would lay down our ray guns, our missiles, our hostility, and open our world to you, little large-headed one, if only you remain.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks at an ultrasound image and sees more than a medical picture. In the dark, grainy space of the scan, the unborn child appears like a mysterious presence floating in a cosmic void. The image suggests both intimacy and distance: the child is inside the mother’s body, yet it also seems to belong to some vast, unknown universe. This makes the moment feel strange, beautiful, and almost otherworldly.

The unborn child is imagined as an alien traveler journeying toward Earth. Hidden within the mother, it seems to be moving through darkness on its way into human life. The speaker pictures the child as a visitor from an unknown place, approaching the world slowly and silently. This image turns pregnancy into a kind of cosmic voyage, with the mother’s body becoming both a shelter and a passageway.

The speaker feels a mixture of anxiety and curiosity. There is a strong desire to make contact with the child, to understand who it is and where it comes from. The child is already deeply loved, but still unknown. Because of this, the speaker’s emotions are complex: wonder, nervousness, longing, and anticipation all exist together. The unborn baby is near enough to be seen, yet still beyond reach.

This encounter also leads the speaker to reflect on profound questions about existence. The ultrasound becomes a symbol of life’s mysteries: where life begins, where it comes from, and what it means to enter the world. The speaker thinks about origins, birth, death, and the boundaries between nothingness and being. The child’s arrival raises questions that cannot be fully answered, but the questions themselves deepen the speaker’s sense of awe.

In the end, the speaker welcomes the child with tenderness and love. Despite the mystery surrounding the baby’s arrival, the speaker offers protection, peace, and care. The child is invited into the world not with fear, but with openness and devotion. The speaker promises to share the Earth with the child, to guard it from harm, and to receive it as a beloved presence entering human life.
outputs.L4:
At first the image is impossible to understand: a storm of gray light, a small weather system moving inside the dark. On the ultrasound screen, the unborn child appears less like a baby than like a message from deep space—flickering, distant, and strange. The room is ordinary, filled with machines and quiet instructions, yet the speaker feels as if they are witnessing something cosmic: a first contact with a life that has traveled from beyond the known world into the hidden universe of the body.

The child is there, but not yet here. Seen only in shadows and pulses, the baby seems alien, a mysterious visitor suspended in a private galaxy. The curve of a spine becomes a constellation. The heartbeat becomes a signal, urgent and miraculous, transmitted across a distance no one can measure. The speaker studies the image with wonder and fear, trying to imagine the person forming inside that darkness. Who are you? What will you become? How can someone be so unknown and already so loved?

Pregnancy, in this vision, is not simple or sentimental. It is awe-filled, but also unsettling. The child is intimate and unreachable at once, a stranger living beneath the mother’s heart. The speaker recognizes the vulnerability of this moment: the fragile body still forming, the uncertain future, the terrifying responsibility of love before arrival. There is anxiety in the waiting, in not knowing what kind of world the child will enter, in understanding how much can be hoped for and how little can be controlled.

And yet the dominant feeling is welcome. The speaker does not need to fully understand the child in order to love them. The mystery does not create distance; it deepens tenderness. This unborn being, glimpsed through static and shadow, is already a presence around which the future begins to gather. The child is both foreign and familiar, both cosmic traveler and family, both unanswered question and beloved answer.

Looking at the ultrasound, the speaker experiences a moment of profound recognition: life begins not as certainty, but as wonder. The child is not yet known by face, voice, or name, but already carries immense meaning. They are a stranger arriving from darkness, and at the same time someone awaited with unconditional devotion. The image on the screen may be blurred and otherworldly, but the feeling it awakens is unmistakable: awe, fear, hope, and a love wide enough to receive the unknown.
outputs.L5:
**Our Milky Way**

The Milky Way is the galaxy we call home. It is a vast system of stars, planets, gas, dust, and dark matter, all held together by gravity. Our Sun is just one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, and Earth is one small planet orbiting it.

The Milky Way has a spiral shape, with long arms stretching out from its center. Our solar system is located in one of these spiral arms, far from the crowded galactic core. On very dark nights, away from city lights, we can see part of the Milky Way as a pale, glowing band across the sky. This light comes from countless distant stars that blend together from our point of view.

At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*. Although it is invisible, scientists study its effects on nearby stars to understand more about it. The galaxy itself is always moving, and our Sun travels around the center of the Milky Way, taking about 225 million years to complete one orbit.

Our Milky Way is only one galaxy among billions in the universe, but it is special to us because it contains our home, our planet, and everything we know. Studying the Milky Way helps us understand where we come from and how the universe works.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem addressed to an unborn baby seen in an ultrasound, using cosmic and science-fiction imagery, playful particle-physics language, and the tone of a prayer or message to an alien visitor.
counterfactuals.output:
Little traveler,

there you are on the monitor—  
a moonlit smudge in the black universe,  
a weather system of milk and starlight,  
curling and uncurling in your private galaxy.

We see you through the snowy telescope of the ultrasound,  
through that soft radar, that hymn-machine,  
which translates your silence into static and silver.  
You flicker like a transmission from a friendly planet.  
You wave—perhaps.  
Or perhaps you are adjusting the controls  
of your tiny spacecraft.

Hello, visitor.  
Hello, comet seed.  
Hello, small astronaut of the blood-dark sea.

May your orbit be gentle.  
May the gravity that holds you be kind.  
May every cell remember the old instructions:  
divide, shimmer, become.  
May your little heart, that red dwarf star,  
keep pulsing its bright Morse code:  
I am, I am, I am.

Already you are practicing miracles  
with no audience but the angels of amniotic fluid.  
You are building fingers out of whispers,  
eyelids out of dusk,  
knees from the secret mathematics of tenderness.  
Quarks of hope are colliding in you.  
Neutrinos of laughter pass through the walls.  
Your mother is the warm observatory,  
the original space station,  
the blue planet humming beneath your sleep.

Do you hear us, small alien?  
We are the beings waiting outside the atmosphere.  
We have prepared blankets, names, lullabies,  
maps of rivers and spoons and morning light.  
We are strange, yes—  
we cry when happy,  
we sing to the dark,  
we keep trying to explain love  
and mostly fail,  
but we are ready to learn your language.

Come in peace when you come.  
Come with your tiny fists full of stardust.  
Come with your wobbling antennae of wonder.  
Come blinking from the portal,  
new citizen of oxygen,  
new theorem of the body,  
new particle in the family field.

Until then, float on, bright speck.  
Dream your zero-gravity dreams.  
Let the universe knit you quietly.  
Let the deep hum bless your bones.

We are listening for you  
across all frequencies.  
We are here,  
beneath the vast and patient stars,  
sending love like a signal  
you can follow home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal monologue from an expectant parent studying an ultrasound printout, imagining the fetus as a little Martian traveling through space toward Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
Look at you.

A gray little weather system. A comma in the static. My bright, grainy cosmonaut folded inside the dark.

The technician says, “Here’s the head,” and points to a moon I am supposed to recognize. “Here’s the spine,” and there it is, a string of tiny signal lights down the black road of you. But I know what I’m seeing. I know a visitor when one flickers on the screen.

You are not floating in fluid. You are traveling through space.

You are a little Martian in a cramped silver ship, knees tucked under your chin, one hand raised as if adjusting a helmet only you can feel. Around you, the universe hums and pulses. My blood is the engine. My heart is mission control, thudding instructions through the walls: keep coming, keep growing, keep your star map close.

I hold this printout like evidence of first contact.

No one else sees the antennae. No one else sees the green of you, because the machine has translated you into shadows, into soft charcoal and snow. But I can imagine you perfectly: serious and luminous, blinking enormous eyes at the red planet you are leaving behind. Maybe you have packed a lunch of comets. Maybe you are wearing boots made from meteor dust. Maybe you are annoyed by the turbulence when I laugh too hard.

Do you know where you’re going?

Earth is strange, little one. It has spoons and thunderstorms. It has doorbells, peaches, parking lots, the smell of rain on concrete. It has people who say “I love you” and then forget to buy milk. It has socks that disappear. It has oceans so large they make even grown humans remember they are temporary.

It also has me.

I don’t know if that is comfort or warning.

I am studying your coordinates, trying to decode the blur of your face. I tilt the paper left, then right, as if the whole future might become legible if I find the correct angle. There: a nose? A fist? A small galactic shrug? You are practicing being mysterious. You are already better at it than I am.

Sometimes I worry you’ll arrive and find the atmosphere unsuitable. Too loud. Too bright. Too heavy with gravity and expectation. I worry your delicate Martian lungs will take one breath of this place and think, No, thank you, I prefer the stars.

But then I imagine you descending anyway.

A tiny capsule through cloud cover. A flare in the night. The hospital room transformed into a landing site. Nurses in orbit. Monitors beeping like satellites. Me, wrecked and astonished, waiting in my paper gown like a farmer watching something impossible burn across the field.

And then you: slippery, furious, alive.

Not a Martian anymore, perhaps. Or perhaps always one. A traveler with a secret passport, stamped in amniotic ink. A citizen of elsewhere who chose, for reasons beyond astronomy, to come here.

I will try to learn your language.

If you speak in cries, I’ll answer in milk and rocking. If you speak in sleep, I’ll guard the perimeter. If you speak in wide-eyed silence at 3 a.m., I’ll sit with you beneath the kitchen light and explain the moon, which you may already know better than I do.

For now, you drift.

For now, you are all possibility and pulse, all curled-up voyage. Your little spacecraft is warm, and I am both planet and sky, both harbor and sea. Every day you travel closer, though neither of us moves in any direction anyone can point to.

Look at you.

My small extraterrestrial.

My postcard from the interior cosmos.

Keep coming. Follow the red thread. Aim for the sound of my voice.

Earth is waiting.

So am I.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, poetic paragraph in the style of contemporary Irish experimental poetry, mixing pregnancy, astronomy, theology, and sci-fi terms like quarks, gravitons, photinos, and ray guns.
counterfactuals.output: In the ninth dark I carry a small republic of starlight, a foetal moon elbowing the tides of my blood, while over the bog the galaxies kneel like old women saying rosaries to a God gone quantum, all sparks and refusals; quarks flicker in the amniotic hush, gravitons tug at the chapel bell, photinos drift through the nave like unborn angels with no faces, and I, mother-ship, monstrance, wet engine of becoming, walk the rain-slick boreen with a ray gun under my coat in case the seraphim turn imperial. The child turns: a comet in its first conspiracy, a psalm written in plasma, a tiny cosmonaut soldering ribs to covenant; and every kick is apocalypse, every craving a supernova of salt, every prayer a failed transmission from Earth to elsewhere, where Mary wears a visor, Patrick pilots a rusted shuttle, and the saints, drunk on dark matter, bless the milk before it arrives.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a whimsical but anxious welcome speech to a baby in the womb, treating the womb as a spacecraft and the child as an extraterrestrial whose arrival might change the world.
counterfactuals.output:
Welcome, tiny traveler.

This is Mission Control speaking from just outside your softly glowing spacecraft, which is currently docked in the warm, mysterious orbit of your mother. We hope your accommodations are adequate: dim lighting, constant room service, a private ocean, and a steady thump-thump-thump to serve as both lullaby and engine noise.

You, little extraterrestrial, have come from the farthest country there is: before. We do not know your customs. We do not yet know whether you prefer moonlight or mashed bananas, whether you will greet Earth with a cry, a yawn, or the solemn expression of an ambassador unimpressed by our atmosphere.

Still, preparations are underway.

We have assembled blankets of questionable folding accuracy. We have tested small socks, though we remain unconvinced anything so tiny can be useful. We have studied car seats with the grave confusion of ancient astronomers. We have filled our home with soft objects, hopeful objects, and several contraptions that beep, rattle, or promise miracles in twelve languages.

We are excited.

We are terrified.

Frankly, your arrival has the potential to disrupt all known systems.

Sleep cycles may collapse. Time may become soup. Ordinary furniture may reveal hidden corners of danger. Adults once believed to be competent may be found at 3:17 a.m. whispering negotiations over a bottle, a diaper, or a mysterious noise from the crib. The cat has not been fully briefed.

And beyond our small station, who can say what you will do?

Perhaps you will arrive and change only everything. Perhaps you will teach stern people to sing nonsense. Perhaps you will turn two hands into a shelter, a room into a planet, a name into a destiny. Perhaps your laugh will cause flowers to file reports. Perhaps your first steps will shift the tides. Perhaps one day you will look at this strange world—its wars, its wonders, its broken clocks and brave bees—and decide to make it kinder.

No pressure.

For now, remain safely aboard your vessel. Float. Grow. Practice your kicks against the inner hull. Send us your encrypted messages in hiccups and rolls. We receive them all with awe and mild alarm.

When you are ready to land, we will be here.

The atmosphere is unstable, the crew is inexperienced, and the planet is not entirely prepared.

But the runway lights are on.

The doors are open.

The world is waiting for its little alien.

And we, your trembling welcoming committee, already love you beyond all maps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a prose poem that begins with someone “scrutinizing the Milky Way” of an ultrasound and develops into a strange prayer of welcome to an unborn “little green man.”
counterfactuals.output:
Scrutinizing the Milky Way of an ultrasound, we lean over the black-and-silver weather of you, the storm-cave, the star-sleet, the small broadcast from the interior planet where you are learning to be a body. You flicker like evidence. You fold and unfold your impossible maps. The nurse points to a comet and calls it a hand, points to a moon and calls it a skull, and all the while you drift there, passenger of the warm dark, our little green man, our visitor from the country before breathing.

Welcome, then, traveler in your watery helmet. Welcome, amphibian prophet, pea-sized emperor, astronaut with no flag but a heartbeat. May the doors of the air not frighten you. May the first light be gentle and the first hunger understandable. May the world, with its huge blue appetite, learn to lower its voice when it speaks to you.

We have prepared nothing worthy of your arrival. Only blankets, names, a room painted the color of a cloud pretending to be calm. Only our hands, which are clumsy birds. Only our hearts, those old engines, knocking and knocking at the border. Forgive us. We have been human a long time and still do not know how to do it without breaking the furniture, the promises, the morning.

Come anyway, little green man. Come with your alien eyes sealed shut, your secret gills, your feet still remembering fins. Come teach us the grammar of beginning again. Come colonize our sleep, our cupboards, our calendars. Come make a small crater in the center of our lives and call it home.

Blessed be the cord, the tether, the silver road. Blessed be the belly’s red planet. Blessed be the static that becomes a face, the nebula that becomes a son, a daughter, a question. Blessed be your soft invasion, your peaceable apocalypse, your tiny, radiant demand.

We are waiting at the edge of your galaxy with milk, with lullabies, with trembling. We are shining every porch light in the universe. Come down. Come in. Take us to your leader, who is you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
